titleStmt.title: A Function for Hard Real-Time System Search-Based Task Mapping Optimisation

analytic.title: A Function for Hard Real-Time System Search-Based Task Mapping Optimisation

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A task mapping is deemed feasible for a hard realtime embedded system if the end-to-end response times of all tasks, which include the computation and the communication delays, does not exceed their deadlines. In this paper, we propose a new fitness function based on the concept of breakdown frequency to address the task mapping optimisation problem of hard realtime embedded systems. As a property of task mapping, the breakdown frequency is the minimal operating frequency under which a task set and its messages are able to execute in any scenario without missing their deadlines. With the frequency, unschedulable tasks and messages can become schedulable without changing the task mapping itself. These advantages are difficult to find in the state-of-the-art optimisation techniques that use the number of unschedulable tasks or latency as the property of task mapping. Results from the case studies suggest that the proposed function enables a wider design space exploration, allowing designers to easily trade-off operating frequency and core count without sacrificing hard real-time schedulability.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Hard real-time embedded systems using Networks-on-Chip (NoC) infrastructure to interconnect processors can become unschedulable when the worst-case end-to-end response time, in which consists of the computation (r i ) and communication (R i ) delays, of at least one of its hard real-time tasks exceeds its deadline. This can happen due to several reasons: the response time of that task is too long because it has to wait for the execution of higher priority tasks, the response time of its messages are too long because they have to go through a long path over the NoC (or they are delayed by congestion), or all happen at the same time. The undesirable result is that the messages may arrive late at the destination task, and this could have catastrophic consequences. For example, brakes will not be activated in time or actuators will use stale data.

The schedulability of a task can be achieved if the platform operating frequency is increased to make its execution and message transmission faster, thus reducing the worst-case endto-end response time and meeting the deadline. The frequency can be further scaled, and the minimal frequency that makes the system fully schedulable is referred to as the breakdown frequency. Notice that the breakdown frequency is a property of a given task mapping, and different task mappings are likely to have different breakdown frequencies because they introduce different interference and congestion patterns which will affect the response time of every task and message and therefore their schedulability. State-of-the-art approaches to hard real-time task mapping problems used the number of unschedulable tasks as the fitness of every mapping. Fig. 1a shows the outcome of the task mapping optimisation process over time, resulting in a schedulable system. Based on this number (shown as schedulability percentage) which was produced by the optimisation algorithm at each point in time, it finally converged to a task mapping whereby all tasks and messages became fully schedulable (100%). Experiment results presented in [1] proved that with a good search-based optimisation heuristic such as Genetic Algorithm (GA), this kind of convergence was possible for a number of benchmarks. However, the results also showed that in some cases a schedulable task mapping cannot be found, and their fitness function did not give any insight on whether this type of mappings actually exists (in those cases, the plot would show a line that never touched the 100% schedulability level).

Our approach to this problem is a new fitness function which can find, for every task mapping, the minimal frequency that makes the system schedulable. Fig. 1b shows the possible outcome of a task mapping optimisation process using the proposed fitness function. The plot shows the breakdown frequency of the task mapping found by the optimisation process at each point in time (normalised to the nominal frequency of the system). Initially, with unoptimised task mappings, the breakdown frequency is likely to be much higher than the nominal frequency, but nonetheless a schedulable mapping is likely to be found (unless starving tasks or messages exist, or the breakdown frequency is higher than what the system can achieve). The optimisation process then tries to minimise the breakdown frequency, so that the system can be schedulable at a lower operating frequency. The point where the plotted curve touches the horizontal line (f = 1) is equivalent to the point where the plotted line touches the 100% schedulability level in Fig. 1a, that is, the optimisation has found a fully schedulable mapping at the nominal frequency. From that point onwards, the optimisation process improves the task mapping even further, lowering its frequency and at the same time maintaining its schedulability, which cannot be properly discriminated by the state-of-the-art fitness function as all task mappings appear to have zero unschedulable tasks. The main technique underlying the calculation of breakdown frequency is a schedulability analysis, which calculates and evaluates the end-to-end response time upper-bound of each task and its messages.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Task mapping is a critical part in complex embedded system design and researchers have proposed several approaches for mapping hard real-time applications in NoC-based embedded systems. For example, [1] performed task mapping based solely on a single objective which was minimising the total number of unschedulable tasks and traffic flows. Other researchers [2] considered multiple objectives such as maximising the robustness and flexibility of task mappings to increase the probability of a task set being schedulable and to accommodate future scenarios. However, these works primarily aimed just at finding schedulable mappings and no further optimisation was performed to scale the systems' operating frequency.

One of the purposes of frequency scaling is to find a minimum frequency at which a task set can execute under specific constraints, but in a hard real-time embedded system, this also include meeting the deadline of its task set. Some researchers proposed a single-processor frequency scaling approach for real-time tasks. While [3] and [4] each presented an approach that could keep the corresponding frequency constant at runtime, [5] proposed an approach for finding multiple speeds of single processor.

Although not many published works focused on optimising task mapping based on frequency scaling for NoC-based multiprocessor hard real-time embedded systems, Shin et al. [6] utilised a GA-based algorithm for assigning the lowest operating speed to links by reducing slack time. In their approach, the communication load on each link was used to determine the worst-case communication delays. However, in the priority pre-emptive hard real-time systems that approach is insufficient because extra delays might be caused by the preemption from high-priority messages. This kind of delays was not considered in their model and this insufficiency limits their approach in minimising frequency for this type of systems.

To achieve predictability in priority-aware NoC based multicore system, a flow-based schedulability analysis [7] was proposed to analyse the worst-case latency of traffic flows. Several extensions to this work were proposed to include the buffer space bounds [8] and the end-to-end response time bound of task [9], [10]. The analysis in [8] provided tight bounds, but they assumed that buffers were arbitrarily large to avoid the back-pressure problem (that is, when a virtual channel has the highest priority over a link, but has no credits because the buffer down the line is full). To avoid this assumption, which can lead to high area and energy dissipation because of potentially large buffer spaces, the schedulability analysis in our approach is based on [7].

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: An application model describes the design-time characteristics of computation and communication load imposed by an application. It consists of a task set and a message set. Two tasks assigned to different cores communicate with each other by sending messages. It is assumed that a task transmits a message only after its execution is complete and the overhead of the network interface is negligible. Before transmission, the packetisation of a message produces one or several packets. A traffic flow represents a series of packets sent over the NoC from a source task to a destination task.

Every task and message are described as T ask = {c, t, p, d} and Msg = {So, De, P, L} tupples respectively. Each task has a worst-case execution time (c), a minimum inter-arrival interval (t), a priority (p) and an end-to-end deadline (d). Each message is sent between a source (So) and a destination (De), has a priority (P ) and a message length (L). The worst-case execution time (WCET, denoted by variable c i ) is the maximum time that a task can take to finish execution when running on its own over a processing core at a given clock frequency (which we refer to as nominal frequency). Several techniques can be used to determine the WCET [11], such as program path analysis and profiling, but the details are beyond the scope of this paper. Likewise, given a specific path over the NoC and a maximum packet size, the basic latency of a message (denoted as C i ) is defined as the maximum time that each of its packets will take to be transferred from source to destination when the NoC is running at the nominal frequency. For most NoCs, the basic latency can be determined, and it is a function of the number of hops, the number of packet flits, the time needed for a flit to traverse a link and the time needed for a router to route and arbitrate packet headers.

We assume that the end-to-end response time upper bound of a task that communicates with other task at a different core includes the amount of time since its release until the last packet sent by it arrives at the receiving task in worst-case scenario. In order to meet the hard real-time constraints, that is, without missing any deadline, the end-to-end response time of a task must be less or equal to the deadline (d), and must never exceed it.

The platform is modelled to represent the architecture of an on-chip multicore system, which uses a NoC as the interconnection. We implemented the platform as a 2D Mesh with a deterministic routing and wormhole switching. The arbitration unit supports flit-level pre-emption to control the access of packets to shared links in accordance with their priorities. A processing core can run more than one task and a link can be shared by multiple traffic flows. The scheduling of tasks and flows is based on a fixed-priority pre-emptive policy [12].

div.head: A. End-to-End Response Time Analysis
div.p: The breakdown frequency fitness function relies on an endto-end response time analysis to validate the schedulability of task and message, and this section explains the equations of the analysis. In our hard real-time system model, based on the priority pre-emptive policy, each task is assigned with a fixed priority level. This is to enable the pre-emption of low-priority tasks by their high-priority counterparts to give the latter tasks guaranteed access to the shared computing resources. Pre-emptive actions create interference and add delays to the response times of tasks with low-priority levels. In order to analyse the worst-case response times of task, the classic schedulability analysis of single processor [13] is applied. This is based on the assumption that each processor has its own priority-ordered queue in accordance with the partitioning scheduling in multiprocessors [14]. Equation ( 1) calculates the worst-case response time (r i ) of task i. If for each task i of a task set, r i ≤ d i , then the task set is deemed schedulable on the processor, where r i and d i are the response time and deadline of task i respectively. The first term of this equation refers to the worst-case execution time (c i ) of task i. The second term refers to the maximum interference experienced by task i, which is caused by a set of high-priority tasks in the interference set (hp(i)) This equation can be solved using an iterative calculation technique [13]. The iteration starts with r 0 i = c i and terminates when r n+1 i = r n i .
div.formula: r n+1 i = c i + ∀T askj ∈hp(i) r n i t j c j (1)
div.p: Similar to tasks, traffic flows on shared NoC links are assigned with fixed priority levels and packets that belong to a traffic flow inherit the same priority as the flow. Routers guarantee access for high-priority packets by pre-empting lowpriority packets from using the shared links. This arbitration policy causes not only direct interference but also indirect interference to packets with low-priority levels. The definition of direct interference is rather straightforward; it is the amount of interference caused by high-priority traffic flows which share the same path as the observed traffic flow i. The indirect interference is caused by the traffic flows with higher priority levels than flows that cause direct interference to the observed traffic flow, sharing the same path with the low-priority flows but not directly with the observed traffic flow. This concept is generalised in equation ( 2), which is derived in [7], to calculate the worst-case latency (R i ) for traffic flow i. The first term of equation ( 2) is the observed flow's basic latency, and the second term refers to the maximum latency caused by the direct and indirect interference of the high-priority flows in the interference set (S D i ). Given a set of traffic flows, this set is deemed schedulable if for each flow i in this set, R i ≤ Q i , where Q i is the deadline of flow i.
div.formula: R n+1 i = C i + ∀F lowj ∈S D i R n i + J R j + J I j T j C j (2)
div.p: We extend the works in [13] and [7] for enabling the end-to-end response time analysis of task. Given a task mapping, the analysis determines whether a task and flow sets are schedulable in the system by validating the end-to-end response time against its deadline. We define the end-to-end response time of a task as the time taken from its release until the last packet it sends is received by the receiving task. To reduce the complexity of the analysis, we assume the deadline of a task as equivalent to its minimum inter-arrival interval (d = t), and the flow share the same deadline as its sending task, hence Q = t.

A task allocated to a core is schedulable if it meets its deadline. However, packets sent by the task to other task at a different core may not necessarily be schedulable if they fail to meet the deadline of their sending task (for example, due to the interference from other packets sharing the same path or to the delay in execution of the task itself). Since we assume that the release of a traffic flow occurs only after the execution of the sending task is complete and the overhead of payload processing in NI is negligible, the release jitter (maximum deviation from release period, denoted as J R ) of the flow can be deduced as the worst-case response time (computation) of the task that releases it. Then, it is immediate that the release jitter is
div.formula: J R = r. A task i is deemed schedulable if r i ≤ d i , whereas a traffic flow is schedulable only if J R i + R i ≤ d i or after substitution r i + R i ≤ d i .
div.p: From equation (2), J I j is referred to as the indirect interference of flow i and appears as the result of pre-emption by the high-priority flows that shared the same path as the flow j but not directly with the observed flow i. Therefore, from equation ( 2):
div.formula: R n+1 i = C i + ∀F lowj ∈S D i R n i + r j + J I j T j C j .(3)
div.p: The worst-case response times of task and the worst-case latency of flow can be calculated by equation ( 1) and (3) respectively. Given that Ut i is the number of unschedulable tasks and Uf i is the number of unschedulable flows, the following comparisons determine if a task set and their respective packet flows are schedulable in the system.
div.formula: T ask i : if r i > d i ⇒ Ut i = 1 F low i : if r i + R i > d i ⇒ Uf i = 1
div.p: The following equation yields the total number of unschedulable tasks and flows, which represents the schedulability of the system.
div.formula: S = k i=1 Ut i + l i=1 Uf i (4)

div.head: B. Breakdown Frequency Metric
div.p: The breakdown frequency is a property (fitness) of a given task mapping, which is the minimal frequency that makes the system schedulable under that mapping. Given a task mapping as input, the Breakdown Frequency (BF) fitness function calculates the metric according to the process flow shown in Fig. 2. It is worth noting that the allocation of tasks on the platform remains unchanged during frequency scaling.

BF selects a frequency value from a finite range of frequencies which is normally used in embedded systems. It is assumed that the selected frequency value represents A standard binary search algorithm is used for scaling a given set of frequencies. The search algorithm is chosen as the scaling algorithm to find the breakdown frequency from the frequency range because it halves the number of items to check in each iteration. This reduces the number of frequency values to test when finding the breakdown frequency. Before scaling, values in the frequency array are sorted in ascending order. The scaling algorithm starts by selecting the middle value from the array and based on this value BF checks the schedulability of all tasks and flows. If the selected frequency value does not make all the tasks and flows schedulable then it selects a new frequency value from the sub-array on the right of the middle element (increase frequency). Otherwise, if they are schedulable, then the scaling algorithm selects a new frequency value from the sub-array on the left of the middle element (decrease frequency). Each iteration (shifting to the left or to the right sub-array) reduces the scope of selection from the array. When no more scaling can be performed, that is, the selection of the middle value returns null, BF returns the breakdown frequency for the task mapping. It is worth noting that the scaling algorithm is not limited to binary search algorithm, any suitable algorithm is applicable.

The schedulability of all tasks and flows is validated using the analysis described in subsection IV-A. This analysis is performed repeatedly every time a frequency value is selected by the scaling algorithm. The output of the analysis is the number of unschedulable tasks and flows, which implies the level of schedulability achieved by the selected frequency for the given task mapping. This information is useful when determining the breakdown frequency of the task mapping. For example, if the number of unschedulable tasks and flows is zero, the metric indicates that the system is schedulable and the scaling algorithm will further reduce the current selected frequency, otherwise it will increase it. If no more frequency setting is available for evaluation, then the lowest frequency that makes the system schedulable is returned as the breakdown frequency of the task mapping. In the case where the breakdown frequency cannot be found at all (for example, because it needs a larger setting than the values in the frequency range), the task mapping will be flagged to indicate it has no breakdown frequency. This is useful for the selection process of task mappings during optimisation.

div.head: C. Task Mapping Optimisation
div.p: In general, the optimisation algorithm explores the design space of the system by generating task mappings, assigns them with fitness values deduced by the fitness function and selects the best task mappings based on their fitness values. Repetition of these processes during the optimisation improves task mappings in a way that minimises their breakdown frequency. With the minimisation of breakdown frequency as the main objective, we chose GA as the optimisation algorithm in our approach as it is widely known for solving optimisation problems. The objective function is defined as equation ( 5), where f is the breakdown frequency of task mapping.

GA represents every solution using the chromosome-like structure, such as shown in Fig. 3. In our approach, the chromosome structure is designed to store information related to task mapping. As shown in the figure, a chromosome is built upon a set of small units called genes. Each gene represents a task and contains a processing core index value (given as an integer number) to which a task will be mapped on the platform.

div.head: A. Test Benches
div.p: In this experimental work we selected several test benches including a realistic application and a few synthetic applications to study the feasibility of the proposed approach in addressing the task mapping optimisation problem. The realistic test bench is called Autonomous Vehicle Application (AVA). It contains 33 tasks for processing data from various sensors and 38 traffic flows to traverse input data from sensors and output data to different actuators in the autonomous vehicle system. The rest of the test benches were synthetically created and numbered from TB-1 to TB-9 according to an increasing order of task set utilisation. Different utilisation was achieved by varying the number of tasks and flows, and the execution time of tasks. Specifically, TB-1 consists of a task set with 625% computing utilisation, TB-2 (724%), TB-3 (975%), TB-4 (1125%), TB-5 (1875%), TB-6 (3850%), TB-7 (5500%), TB-8 (6500%) and TB-9 (7500%). From TB-1 to TB-5, each contained a set of messages with 1075% communication utilisation, whilst from TB-6 to TB-9 each had 8488%. Every task had a unique priority and a flow inherited the same priority as its sending task. Different size of platforms, 4x4, 5x5 and 10x10 mesh NoCs were prepared for mapping the test benches and each platform could support 1600%, 2500% and 10000% processors utilisation respectively.

div.head: B. Baselines
div.p: The purpose of this experimental work was to study the performance of the Breakdown Frequency (BF) fitness function and to demonstrate that a task mapping optimisation algorithm integrated with BF could find a schedulable task mapping, not only at the nominal frequency but also below that level. In order to show the improvement achieved by the proposed fitness function, the Schedulability (SC) fitness function from previous work [1] was implemented to provide the schedulability metric as the property of task mapping. The difference between both functions is described as follows:
• BF yields the breakdown frequency as task mapping property
• SC yields the number of unschedulable tasks and flows as task mapping property

We chose a generic GA and created 2 different algorithms by integrating BF and SC with it, hereafter called as GA-BF and GA-SC algorithms respectively. The main difference between GA-SC and GA-BF is their optimisation objectives. The GA-SC's objective was to minimise the number of unschedulable tasks and flows while the objective of GA-BF was to minimise the breakdown frequency of the system. Both algorithms were configured with the same settings as reported in [15]: 100 population size, 500 maximum generations, 0.5 crossover rate and 0.01 mutation rate.

div.head: C. Results
div.p: The experimental hypothesis states that GA-BF is better in finding the schedulable task mapping than GA-SC. In a 4x4 platform, both GA-BF and GA-SC could find a schedulable task mapping for AVA at the nominal frequency, as depicted in Fig. 4a. Although both algorithms successfully converged to 100% schedulability between 10 and 100 generations, GA-SC's performance was faster than GA-BF. The faster convergence shown by GA-SC could be generated from the direct minimisation of the schedulability metric, which is the number of unschedulable tasks and flows, thus optimising the task mappings at the nominal frequency was rather straightforward. Contrarily, GA-BF had a different optimisation objective than GA-SC, the task mappings were evolved according to the minimisation of breakdown frequency. At the beginning of the optimisation, the breakdown frequency was usually higher than the nominal frequency. To reach the nominal level, GA-BF had to scale the breakdown frequency and at the same time maintained the schedulability of the system. Nonetheless, both were comparably good in finding the schedulable task mapping at the nominal frequency and were able to converge in less than 100 generations. Moreover, Fig. 4b shows that GA-BF converged below the nominal level, which is a significant improvement as compared to GA-SC, which could only find the schedulable task mapping at the nominal level (Fig. 4a). GA-BF could find a schedulable task mapping early during the optimisation if a breakdown frequency exists, but at the expense of time overhead when scaling the frequency for each task mapping. The overhead affects the optimisation algorithm run-time because finding the breakdown frequency of task mapping requires validating all tasks and flows for every selected frequency. Based on AVA test bench, Fig. 5 shows GA-BF consumed more time than GA-SC to complete in 500 generations. It is also depicted in the same figure that the cumulative time difference between GA-BF and GA-SC was significant. Nonetheless, GA-BF found the schedulable task mapping at the nominal frequency early during the optimisation, which is indicated by point 'K' in the graph. The rest of the time was spent for reducing the breakdown frequency further below the nominal level.

In spite of the time overhead, GA-BF facilitated the task mapping optimisation process by finding the breakdown frequencies which makes the task mappings schedulable. By using test benches TB-1 to TB-6 and mapped them onto the 4x4 and 5x5 platforms, the lowest breakdown frequency was recorded at each point in time from the first to the last generation. The results are shown by graphs in Fig. 6a and Fig. 6b. In each of the graphs a horizontal black line (y = 1) is drawn to represent the nominal frequency level. As shown in Fig. 6a, GA-BF successfully found the breakdown frequency for at least one task mapping in every generation. In other words, the task mapping found by GA-BF was feasible for the system even at the early stage of optimisation. Furthermore, GA-BF maintained the schedulability while gradually scaled down the breakdown frequency towards the nominal level.

Expanding the size of platform to 5x5 for mapping the same test benches used for the 4x4 platform saw GA-BF successfully converged below the nominal frequency, as depicted in Fig. 6b. It is worth noting that with a larger platform it was easier for GA-SC to find a schedulable task mapping, but the schedulability is limited at the nominal frequency. In fact, GA-BF offered better advantages; all tasks and flows of the test benches were schedulable below the nominal frequency except for TB-5 and TB-6. Similar as the 4x4 platform, at the beginning of optimisation the breakdown frequency was higher than the nominal level, but as the optimisation progressed the algorithm converged to the nominal level and subsequently fell below it.

In some cases such as when a task set with large utilisation exists, mapping it to smaller platforms using GA-SC made the system hardly schedulable. As an example, this can be shown using two synthetic test benches (TB-4 and TB-6), with each mapped onto the 4x4 and 5x5 platforms. The results shown in Fig. 7a and Fig. 8a show how many tasks and flows were schedulable with GA-SC. Fig. 7a shows that GA-SC achieved less than 80% schedulability for TB-4 and less than 35% for TB-6. For a hard real-time system, achieving 100% schedulable tasks and flows is essential to ensure the predictability of the system, but in these cases GA-SC's task mappings were unfeasible for the system. Despite increasing the platform size to simply make the task mapping easier for GA-SC, GA-BF provided a better way of improving the task mapping optimisation process through the minimisation of breakdown frequency. The plot depicted in Fig. 7b shows how GA-BF converged, even though above the nominal level, its task mapping at each point in time was schedulable and feasible for the system.

It should be noted that a 5x5 platform consists more computation and communication resources than a 4x4 platform, reducing the number of shares in a resource and providing chances for low-priority tasks and flows to evade interference. As a result, GA-SC successfully converged to 100% schedulability with TB-4 test bench as depicted in Fig. 8a. With a larger platform the mapping was less difficult for GA-SC, but its task mappings were only usable at the nominal frequency. In fact, GA-SC failed to find any schedulable task mapping for TB-6. GA-BF addressed this task mapping optimisation problem by finding the breakdown frequency for the given task mappings, improving them to become feasible for the system. As shown in Fig. 8b the algorithm converged below the nominal level with TB-4 and slightly above the level with TB-6.

GA-BF showed a consistent performance when mapping higher utilisation task sets onto a larger platform. Test benches TB-7, TB-8 and TB-9 were mapped onto a 10x10 platform to observe its performance. Results depicted in Fig. 9a show that GA-SC failed to find any feasible task mapping for the system, even in a platform with greater number of processors. Conversely, GA-BF showed better performance outperforming GA-SC; the task mapping found at each point of time was schedulable, though the frequency was above the nominal level.

The results presented in this section suggest that GA-BF is better in finding schedulable task mappings than GA-SC for the given test benches, and this validates the experimental hypothesis stated earlier in this section.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: An unfeasible task mapping from an optimisation process can be improved if the breakdown frequency that makes all tasks and messages schedulable is found. Finding the frequency, however, is not a simple matter due to the fact that different task mappings introduce various interference patterns. Without an appropriate frequency-scaling technique suitable for hard real-time task mapping optimisation, merely lowering the frequency will only delay the end-to-end response time. The breakdown frequency at which the system could become schedulable is essential for the system to avoid unnecessary any increment of the operating frequency. A new fitness function is proposed to find the breakdown frequency for addressing the task mapping optimisation problem. If the breakdown frequency can be found for a given task mapping, the system will definitely be schedulable regardless the initial feasibility of the task mapping. Furthermore, applying the breakdown frequency, as the property of task mapping in a task mapping optimisation process, improves the quality of task mappings more effectively. Although the optimisation process could reap the benefits offered by the new approach, the process of finding the breakdown frequency is still an iterative operation. For every selected frequency, all tasks and messages need to be evaluated to determine their schedulability, and this increases the run-time of the optimisation algorithm. In future work, we will study the performance of the breakdown frequency fitness function in multi-objective optimisation, considering other metrics such as power dissipation to give a broader insight on the impact of the approach to the system.
